Secondly, you'll forgive me if I don't take you on your word about your self diagnosis of having food addiction, and I especially have a few words to say concerning the part about you feeling like shit while not eating. For starters, overweight people often demonstrate a lack of understanding about hunger. More specifically, the difference between actual hunger and what is commonly referred to as "emotional hunger", aka "psychological hunger", which is the desire to eat when you're already full. Let's be blunt about what this is. It's the pleasure seeking desire with relation to food. It's not real hunger. It's simply wanting to eat things because they're enjoyable to eat. This is primarily what makes people become massively overweight. There's also a delay between when you're full and when the brain registers it, and that's the source of SOME overeating, but if someone is obese, their desire to eat obviously goes above and beyond hunger and that delay.

Simply wanting to be able to do something that feels good really badly and not being able to do it can be one of the worst feelings. It can make you sick to your stomach. It can make you constantly obsess about it. Everybody remembers what the days leading up to Christmas used to be like as a kid. They were torturous. That's just one time a year. Twice a year if you count birthdays. Now imagine that you've had a constant source of pleasure almost your whole life, and you made full use of it. Then suddenly, someone takes it away. How would you feel? In your case, you don't have to imagine. You remember how bad it would feel when you weren't able to eat.

Tell me how this equates to it being an addiction. What I see is a child that always got his way when it came to food. Whenever that child had their comfort blanket torn away, he felt awful. All he wanted to do was put it back on. Then that child grew into a man, and as a man, he put away his blanket. It wasn't easy, but he did it.

Addiction is a tempting and convenient shorthand to use. But as far as I can tell, that's all it is.

edit: I thought of an even simpler analog. What happens when you take away a baby's pacifier? It cries. Why does it cry? Suddenly not having the pacifier feels bad. Crying is likely to get it returned. Is the baby addicted to the pacifier? No, of course not. You could only say that in the loosest sense of the word. And yet you'll probably still hear people say "he/she is addicted to that thing". Do we need to set up pacifier rehabilitation centers? Pacifierholics anonymous? No.
